blocks.text: The previous lesson introduced the JSON-RPC envelope in broad strokes, jsonrpc, id, method, params. This lesson zooms all the way in on just one of those three message kinds, the request, and looks closely at how a real MCP request gets built, what its method names actually look like in practice, how params is structured for different operations, and what job the id field is doing every single time a request goes out.
1. The Anatomy of a Request

blocks.alt: jsonrpc, id, method, and params make up a request
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738928-992594297.png

If any of these four fields is missing where it should be present, most servers will reject the message rather than trying to guess intent, jsonrpc must be exactly 2.0, id must be present for anything expecting a reply, method must be a valid string the server recognizes, and params, while sometimes optional in theory, is best always included.

A JSON-RPC request that MCP recognizes has exactly four fields, no more and no fewer, jsonrpc fixed at 2.0, id chosen by whoever is sending the request, method naming the operation being invoked, and params carrying whatever arguments that operation needs. Every request you will ever see in MCP, from the very first initialize call to the last tools/call before a session ends, follows this same four-field shape.

It helps to think of method as the verb and params as the object of that verb, method says what to do, params says what to do it with or to. Getting comfortable reading requests this way, verb first, then arguments, makes even unfamiliar method names easier to guess the shape of.
2. Method Naming Conventions

blocks.alt: tools/call and resources/read follow the same naming convention
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738928-29638447.png
2.1 Category Names Match the Concepts You Already Know

The categories in method names, tools, resources, prompts, are not arbitrary, they map directly onto the three core MCP concepts covered in the MCP Fundamentals module. If you already understand what a tool, a resource, and a prompt are conceptually, the method name categories should feel completely unsurprising rather than like new vocabulary to memorize.

MCP method names follow a consistent category slash action pattern, tools/list, tools/call, resources/read, prompts/get, and so on. The part before the slash names the category of thing being operated on, tools, resources, prompts, and the part after the slash names the specific action within that category, list, call, read, get, subscribe.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Category","Typical actions"],"rows":[["tools","list, call"],["resources","list, read, subscribe, unsubscribe"],["prompts","list, get"],["(session level)","initialize, ping"]]}

blocks.text: This naming discipline exists so that a developer scanning a log of method names can immediately guess what a message is about even without memorizing the full method list, tools/call obviously calls a tool, resources/read obviously reads a resource. Compare that to an alternative where every operation got an arbitrary numeric code, readability would suffer enormously.
3. Why Not Just Use One Generic Method Name

There is a secondary benefit too, distinct method names make it possible for a server to advertise exactly which operations it supports as part of its declared capabilities, rather than exposing one giant catch-all endpoint and leaving the client to guess what params shapes are actually accepted.
An alternative design might have used a single method name, say execute, with a params field describing what to execute, similar to how some older RPC systems work.

MCP deliberately avoided that, having distinct method names for distinct operations means a server can validate and route requests before even looking inside params, and it means MCP's specification can describe each operation's params and result shape independently, rather than describing one giant polymorphic params blob that changes shape depending on some inner discriminator field.

This also plays nicely with how servers are typically implemented, a server's request handling code usually branches on the method string very early, often with a straightforward switch statement or handler registry, dispatching tools/call to one function and resources/read to a completely different one. Distinct method names make that dispatch trivial.
4. The params Object

blocks.alt: A method carries a params object
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738929-693716440.png
4.1 params Always Matches a Documented Shape

Nothing about params is improvised on the fly, whatever a method expects is fixed by the MCP specification, or, for tools/call specifically, by the inputSchema a tool declared for itself during discovery. A client should never have to guess what fields belong in params, it should always be reading that shape from either the spec or the server's own advertised schema.

params is where a request's actual arguments live, and its shape depends entirely on which method is being called. For tools/call, params always includes a name field, identifying which tool to run, and an arguments field, an object whose shape matches whatever inputSchema that particular tool declared during discovery.

Some methods need very little in params, tools/list often sends an empty object, since there is nothing to specify beyond just asking for the list. Others, like resources/read, need just enough to identify what is being requested, typically a single uri field.
5. params Can Be Omitted or Empty, But Rarely Entirely Absent

A quick sanity check some client libraries run before sending anything, if a method is documented as taking no arguments and params is not an empty object, treat that as a bug in the calling code rather than assuming the server will silently tolerate it.

The JSON-RPC specification technically allows params to be omitted entirely when a method needs no arguments, but in practice most MCP implementations still send an empty object, params colon curly braces, rather than dropping the field. This is partly a matter of convention and partly because some client and server libraries expect params to always be present, even if empty, to keep their parsing code simpler.

If you are implementing an MCP client or server yourself, the safest choice is to always include params, using an empty object when there is nothing to send, rather than relying on every counterpart correctly handling its absence.
6. The id Field's Role in a Request

blocks.alt: A request id correlates the response
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738929-871340443.png

It is worth stating plainly, id has nothing to do with identifying a tool, a resource, or any application-level concept, it only ever identifies one particular request-response exchange on one particular connection. Do not confuse a request's id with, say, a resource's uri or a tool's name, they operate at completely different layers.

Every request carries an id chosen by the sender, and that id's entire purpose is to let the sender later recognize which response answers which request. The receiver never invents or changes the id, it simply copies the exact same value into its eventual response.

Because a connection can have several requests outstanding at once, pipelined one after another without waiting for replies in between, the id is what makes it possible to sort out which reply belongs to which question once responses start arriving, potentially out of order. The Message IDs lesson later in this module goes much deeper on the exact rules, this lesson focuses on how id shows up structurally inside a request.
7. Choosing Sensible ids

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Pros","Cons"],"rows":[["Incrementing integer","Simple, readable logs","Needs a single shared counter"],["Random UUID string","No coordination needed across components","Longer, less readable logs"]]}

blocks.text: Most MCP client implementations use a simple incrementing counter, starting at 1 and going up by one for every new request sent on a given connection. This is simple, guarantees uniqueness for the lifetime of that connection, and makes debugging logs easy to read, since ids climb in a predictable order.

Some clients instead use randomly generated strings or UUIDs, which avoids any risk of accidental collision across multiple independent request-issuing components sharing one connection, at the cost of slightly less readable logs. Either approach is valid, JSON-RPC only requires uniqueness among currently outstanding requests, not any particular format.
8. The initialize Request, a Special Case

blocks.alt: The initialize request must come first
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738930-871386643.png
8.1 initialize Is Still Just a Request

Despite its special role opening every session, initialize is not a different message type, it is an ordinary JSON-RPC request with an id and a matching response expected, exactly like tools/call or resources/read. What makes it special is purely a convention, both sides agree it must be the very first request sent, before any other method is used.

Every MCP session opens with exactly one special request, initialize, and its params look a little different from a typical tools or resources call. Instead of naming an operation on some category of object, it carries the client's own protocol version and declared capabilities, information the server needs before either side can safely talk about tools, resources, or prompts at all.

The Protocol Versioning lesson later in this module explores protocolVersion in depth, and the MCP Architecture module's capability-negotiation lesson covers what capabilities actually declares. For now, notice that this is still an ordinary JSON-RPC request, jsonrpc, id, method, params, just with a params shape specific to starting a session rather than operating on a tool or resource.
9. Requests That List Things

blocks.alt: A client sends tools/list to get a list of items
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738930-231336627.png

Notice that even though a list request's params can be nearly empty, it still goes through the exact same envelope, the same id assignment, the same jsonrpc field, as a far more complex tools/call. Consistency of the envelope regardless of how simple or complex the operation is one of the quieter benefits of building MCP on JSON-RPC.

A whole family of MCP requests exist purely to ask a server what it has available, tools/list, resources/list, prompts/list. These share a common shape, minimal or empty params, and often support an optional cursor field in params for paginated results when a server has more items than fit comfortably in one response.

Pagination through cursor is covered in depth in the Resource Pagination lesson of the MCP Resources module, mentioned here only to show that even a simple-looking list request can carry meaningful params once a server has enough items to need paging.
10. Requests That Act on a Specific Named Thing

blocks.alt: A client sends tools/call to perform a specific named action
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785439738931-261781532.png
One more identifying-field example worth seeing directly, a resources/read request naming a specific file by its uri, the simplest possible named-thing request in MCP.

Unlike the list family, requests such as tools/call, resources/read, and prompts/get all need to identify one specific thing to act on, a tool name, a resource uri, or a prompt name. These requests always include that identifying field directly inside params, alongside any additional arguments the operation needs.

Spotting this pattern, list methods need little or nothing, named-thing methods need an identifier, makes it much easier to guess the shape of a params object for any method you have not seen documented yet.
11. Validating a Request Before Sending It

items: Check every field the schema marks as required is present in arguments.
Check each field's type roughly matches, a number where a number is expected, a string where a string is expected.
Check for fields the schema does not recognize at all, which often indicates a typo in the calling code.

blocks.text: A well-behaved client checks a tool's declared inputSchema, learned earlier during tools/list, before ever sending a tools/call request, catching missing or malformed arguments locally rather than making a round trip only to receive an error response back. This validation step happens entirely on the client side, before params is even built, and it is one of the most common places real MCP client implementations invest engineering effort.

Skipping this step does not break anything structurally, an invalid request will simply come back with an error response instead, but validating early saves a network round trip and gives faster feedback, especially valuable when a model is iterating quickly through several tool calls in a row.
12. Requests Can Nest Complex params

This flexibility is exactly why MCP tools can model such a wide range of real-world operations, from a single-argument lookup to a deeply structured multi-step booking, without the request envelope itself ever needing to change shape to accommodate them.

Nothing limits params to flat key-value pairs, arguments inside a tools/call request can be arbitrarily nested JSON, arrays, nested objects, whatever shape the tool's inputSchema describes. A tool that books a multi-leg trip, for instance, might expect an array of leg objects, each with its own origin, destination, and date fields.

The request envelope itself, jsonrpc, id, method, params, never changes regardless of how deeply nested the actual arguments get, only the contents of params grow more elaborate as a tool's inputs become more complex.
13. Requests Versus Notifications, Structurally

blocks.title: A quick way to check
blocks.content: If you are staring at a message and unsure whether it is a request or a notification, look for the id field first, present means request, absent means notification, this single check resolves the ambiguity every time.

blocks.text: A request and a notification can look almost identical, both have jsonrpc, method, and params, the only structural difference is that a request has an id and a notification does not. This tiny difference carries enormous meaning, it is the entire signal that tells the receiving side whether a reply is expected.

The Notifications lesson later in this module explores the receiving side of that distinction in depth, this lesson's job was just to make sure the sending side, building the request itself, is second nature first.
14. Reading Method Names You Have Never Seen Before

This readability is not an accident, it reflects a deliberate design goal of MCP, that a person reading raw traffic between a client and server should be able to follow along at a glance, without needing a lookup table open in another window for every single method name encountered.

Because MCP's naming pattern is so consistent, category slash action, encountering an unfamiliar method name in a trace, say completion/complete or logging/setLevel, gives you a solid first guess at what it does even before checking documentation. completion suggests something about auto-completing a value, setLevel under logging suggests adjusting how verbose a server's logs are.

This is a small thing, but over the course of working with MCP servers built by many different teams, being able to read an unfamiliar request's intent from its method name alone, without stopping to look anything up, saves real time.
Worked Example: Building a Request From Scratch

Try the same exercise again but for a tool that needs no arguments at all, say a get_server_time tool, notice how much of the same request shape stays identical, only arguments shrinks down to an empty object.

Suppose you are writing client code that needs to call a translate_text tool, which its inputSchema says requires a text field and a target_language field. Walk through constructing the request step by step.

Every step maps directly back to a section in this lesson, method naming from section 2, the params shape for a named-thing operation from section 10, and id assignment from section 7. Building requests by hand like this a few times is the fastest way to make the shape feel automatic.
Common Mistakes

items: Sending params as a bare value instead of an object, MCP always expects params to be a JSON object, even when it only wraps one field.
Forgetting the arguments wrapper inside tools/call params, and putting tool arguments directly under params instead of nested under params.arguments.
Reusing an id that is still awaiting a response, which makes it impossible for the receiver's reply to be matched back correctly.
Skipping client-side validation against a tool's inputSchema, then being surprised by an error response that a quick local check would have caught first.
Assuming every method needs elaborate params, many, like tools/list, genuinely need nothing beyond an empty object.
Guessing at a method name instead of checking what the server actually advertised during discovery, method names are not universal across every server, though naming conventions are consistent.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Hint
blocks.content: max_words is optional, so your filled-in arguments object can include it or leave it out, both are valid requests, the difference just reflects whether the caller wants to constrain the summary length.

blocks.text: Write, by hand, the full JSON-RPC request for calling a hypothetical tool named summarize_article, which requires a url argument and accepts an optional max_words argument. Choose your own id, following the incrementing convention from this lesson.

Once you have filled it in, check it against section 1's anatomy checklist, all four envelope fields present, params correctly wrapping name and arguments, and an id that has not been used by any other outstanding request on this imagined connection.
Key Takeaway

A request is a JSON-RPC envelope carrying jsonrpc, id, method, and params, where method follows a consistent category slash action naming convention and params holds whatever arguments that specific operation needs, from nothing at all for a plain list call to deeply nested arguments for a complex tool. The id exists purely so the sender can later match an eventual response back to this exact request, especially once several requests are in flight at once.

The next lesson, Response Messages, turns to the other side of that pairing, looking closely at how a server structures its reply, how the same id reappears to close the loop, and how the result shape differs depending on which kind of request it is answering.
